The argument for Compliance-as-code ends audit theater is simple: decisions made on stale information cost more than the platform that would make them current — and the gap is measurable in weeks, not years.

items: One framework-agnostic control register maps to SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS 4.0 and DORA simultaneously.
Failing-control workflows matter more than dashboards: findings need owners and dates.
DORA's third-party oversight is a data problem; treat the register as a governed product.

blocks.x: Three questions to ask your current vendors

items: Ask for the baseline: how was the starting position measured, and who signed it?
Ask for the trail: can your auditors replay any decision the system made last week, end to end?
Ask for the unit cost: what does one decision cost to run, and who owns keeping it down?

blocks.x: The honest list of where Compliance-as-code ends audit theater programs go wrong: no signed baseline, gates without stop authority, evidence reconstructed after the fact. Each has a named guard in the sections above.

items: Every stage has a gate with real stop authority — scope expands on measured deltas, not on momentum.
The operating model is designed first — who decides what, at which gate, holding which evidence.
Evidence is generated while the work happens, so the audit is a walkthrough, not an archaeology project.

blocks.x: Audit preparation effort typically falls 60-80% under evidence automation.
Where this shows up in our work
Compliance-as-code ends audit theater shows up in our work wherever a decision is repeated enough for measurement to matter and regulated enough for evidence to be mandatory.
